passage: Throughout most of human history, literacy was defined as the ability to decode printed text and construct clear written arguments. Today, however, rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence require expanding that definition to include algorithmic literacy. When students and professionals rely on automated tools to draft essays, summarize research, or write software code, they risk mistaking fluent, confident prose for verified truth. Because large language models predict plausible word sequences rather than verifying facts against reality, they can fabricate citations, overlook subtle context, or reproduce hidden biases in their training data. Cultivating algorithmic literacy means training users to interrogate machine outputs critically, cross-check claims against primary sources, and understand how statistical models operate. Only by combining human judgment with technological fluency can individuals remain active thinkers rather than passive consumers of automated content.
